entries.meaning: Beholding the Lord, the demon host could not loose its arrows and stood transfixed. Khara and Dūṣaṇa summoned their ministers and said, ‘This is no ordinary person but a princely youth, an ornament among men. We have seen, conquered and slain many serpents, demons, gods, human beings and sages, yet in our whole lives, brothers, we have never seen such beauty. Though he has disfigured our sister, this incomparable man does not deserve death. Tell the two brothers: “Surrender your woman at once, then depart alive for your home.” Report my words and return quickly with their reply.’ The messengers went and spoke to Rāma, who heard and smiled: ‘We are kṣatriyas hunting in the forest and roam in search of wicked beasts like you. Seeing a powerful enemy, we do not fear; we would fight even Time itself once. Though human youths, we destroy demon lineages, protect sages and punish villains. If you have no strength, turn home: I kill no one who withdraws from battle. To mount the battlefield and then practise deceit against an enemy is extreme cowardice disguised as cleverness.’ The messengers immediately reported everything; hearing it, Khara and Dūṣaṇa burned intensely within.

The demons then advanced, knowing their arrows to be terrible and hissing like many serpents. Enraged in battle, Śrī Rāma moved forward with perfectly sharp arrows. Seeing those exceedingly keen shafts, the demon heroes turned. The three brothers angrily decreed that whoever fled the battlefield would be killed by their own hands; resolving to die, the warriors returned and attacked from the front with many kinds of weapons. Knowing the enemy supremely enraged, the Lord set arrows to his bow and released a great shower of iron shafts that began cutting down the fearsome demons. Chests, heads, arms, hands and feet fell everywhere upon the earth; struck by arrows, the shrieking warriors dropped like mountains. Bodies were cut into a hundred pieces, yet rose again through magical fraud; arms and heads flew through the sky and headless trunks ran. Vultures, herons, crows and jackals snapped terribly; jackals, ghosts, spirits and demons gathered skulls, while vetālas and heroes beat skulls like cymbals and yoginīs danced. Rāma's fierce arrows severed warriors' chests, arms and heads; they fell everywhere, rose to fight and cried fearfully, ‘Seize him!’ Vultures flew clutching entrails, and demons ran gripping them, as though children in the city of battle were flying many kites. Warriors were slain, thrown down and pierced through the chest, falling in great numbers with groans. Seeing their own army distraught, Khara, Dūṣaṇa, Triśirā and the other champions turned back. In one instant innumerable demons angrily hurled arrows, lances, javelins, axes, tridents and swords at Rāma. The Lord instantly countered the hostile shafts and struck back with arrows, planting ten in the chest of every demon commander. Falling, rising, clashing and dying, the warriors produced dense illusion; the gods feared at seeing fourteen thousand demons against Ayodhyā's sole lord. Seeing the gods and sages afraid, Rāma, master of māyā, performed a great wonder: each foe saw Rāma in every other foe, fought his own companions, and died.

When Rāma conquered his enemies in battle, the fear of gods, humans and sages ended. Lakṣmaṇa then brought Sītā; falling at the Lord's feet, he was joyfully embraced. Sītā gazed upon Rāma's gentle dark body, and her eyes, filled with supreme love, could not be satisfied. Dwelling at Pañcavaṭī, Rāma performed deeds that gave joy to gods and sages. Seeing the smoke from Khara and Dūṣaṇa's destruction, Śūrpaṇakhā went and incited Rāvaṇa. Speaking in intense anger she reproached him: ‘You drink and sleep day and night, forgetting country and treasury, unaware of the enemy over your head. Sovereignty without statecraft, wealth without dharma, righteous action not offered to Hari, and learning acquired without discernment—all labour spent reading and attaining these bears no fruit. An ascetic is ruined by company, a king by evil counsel, knowledge by pride, modesty by drink, love without humility, and a virtuous person by arrogance; such, I have heard, is the rule. Enemy, disease, fire, sin, master and serpent should never be considered small.’ Having said this and lamented in many ways, she began to weep. Falling distraught in the middle of the court, she cried, ‘Ten-headed one, can such a fate be mine while you still live?’

Hearing her, the courtiers rose in alarm, took her arm, lifted and consoled her. Rāvaṇa asked her to tell what had happened and who had cut off her nose and ears. She replied, ‘Two sons of Daśaratha, king of Ayodhyā—lions among men—have come to sport in the forest. Their conduct has made me understand that they will rid the earth of demons. Protected by the strength of your arms, ten-headed one, sages used to roam the forest without fear; now, though looking like boys, these two are equal to Time, supremely steadfast archers of many virtues, incomparable in strength and splendour, intent on killing villains and givers of happiness to gods and sages. One is the abode of beauty named Rāma. With them is a dark-complexioned woman whom the Creator has fashioned as a treasury of beauty; a hundred crore Ratis would be sacrificed before her. Rāma's younger brother cut off my ears and nose when he heard me mocked as your sister. Hearing my cry, Khara and Dūṣaṇa attacked, but within a moment the brothers killed their whole army.’ On hearing of the death of Khara, Dūṣaṇa and Triśirā, Rāvaṇa's whole body burned. He consoled Śūrpaṇakhā and boasted of his strength in many ways, but went home in deep anxiety and could not sleep that night.

Rāvaṇa reflected: ‘Among gods, humans, demons, serpents and birds there is none who can oppose my follower. Khara and Dūṣaṇa were as strong as I; who could kill them except God? If the Lord has taken incarnation to delight the gods and relieve the earth's burden, I will stubbornly go and make enmity with him, abandon life under his arrow, and cross the ocean of becoming. This tamasic body will not produce devotion—this is my firm resolve in mind, deed and speech. If he is merely a king's son in human form, I shall abduct his woman and conquer both in battle.’ He went alone by aerial car to the place where Mārīca lived beside the ocean. Meanwhile hear, Umā, the lovely plan that Rāma made. When Lakṣmaṇa had gone into the forest to gather roots, fruits and tubers, Rāma, smiling treasury of grace and joy, spoke to Janaka's daughter.

Rāma said, ‘Hear me, beloved, virtuous and fair in your vows. I shall enact a charming human drama. Dwell within fire until I have destroyed the demons.’ The moment Rāma explained everything, Sītā held the Lord's feet in her heart and entered the fire, leaving there her own exact reflection—equally virtuous, beautiful and modest. Even Lakṣmaṇa did not know this secret or any of the divine drama the Lord devised. The ten-headed Rāvaṇa reached Mārīca, bowed his head though the villain was absorbed in selfish purpose, and addressed him with pleasing speech. The bending of a wicked person is intensely painful—like the bend of hook, bow, serpent or cat. A villain's pleasant words inspire fear, Bhavānī, like flowers blooming out of season. Mārīca respectfully honoured him and asked, ‘Father, for what reason is your mind so agitated that you have come here unusually?’
